## The remote-access line in VAL-1203's statement of work

The vendor's implementation consultant has a new ask for VAL-1203. Buried in a statement-of-work
addendum: once Release B goes live, the consultant wants **persistent remote access** to the
central BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) application server — not just during
cutover, but afterward, "to reduce mean time to resolution on any post-go-live issue." Standing
credentials, no stated expiration.

You've seen this movie before, and so has Quality. Earlier in your tenure, this same vendor's
remote-support platform was the subject of a security incident — nothing BECS-specific was
compromised, but it's the reason anyone here flinches at "the vendor wants a standing connection."
And a formal vendor risk assessment on this vendor, VRA-0219, found something uncomfortable: the
vendor's own confident claim — "yes, we notify customers in advance of any change" — didn't survive
a check against the deviation log, which showed a change that arrived with no advance notice at
all. The consultant, reasonably, doesn't expect you to bring either one up. You're going to anyway.

Here's the question sitting on your desk, and it isn't a simple yes/no: if the vendor gets standing
remote access to BECS, is BECS still what FDA's electronic-records regulation calls a **"closed
system"** — or has it become something else, with a heavier set of obligations attached?

A second thread, quieter but just as real, is sitting in VAL-1203's URS (user requirements
specification), revised once already after module 1 sent it back for an untestable row and a
missing risk ranking. What it still doesn't have is any row that says, in testable language, "BECS
refuses to release a component before all required results are recorded" or "BECS refuses a
release attempted by a role not authorized to perform it." Those behaviors are almost certainly
true of the software. Nobody has written a test that tries to make BECS fail at either one. No
citations yet — just notice both gaps are shaped the same way: a real capability nobody has
required the system to prove it has.

## Why this distinction exists, and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to head off: a validated system that quietly stops being the
system Lakeshore validated, because control over who can touch it drifted to someone outside
Lakeshore's own accountability chain — without anyone treating that drift as a change worth a
second look. A vendor with standing, unlogged, unrevokable access to a production BECS server
isn't a security nicety to tighten later. It's a fact about who actually controls the electronic
records on that system, and "who controls the records" turns out to be the exact question Part 11
asks.

You already run the ITSM (IT service management) vocabulary for this shape of problem. **IAM
(identity and access management) and RBAC (role-based access control)** are what you already use
to decide who gets what level of access to any system, and why. **PAM (privileged access
management)** is the tighter discipline you already apply to admin-level accounts specifically:
time-bound checkouts, logged sessions, no standing credentials sitting around waiting to be
misused. **Workflow enforcement inside an ITSM tool** — a change ticket that literally cannot be
closed before the required approval step has actually happened, because the tool enforces the
sequence, not because a policy document says it should — is a pattern you rely on constantly. The
closed-vs-open-system question bridges to something every IT leader already asks about any **SaaS
(software as a service)** or vendor-hosted arrangement: **who holds admin control of the tenant?**
A vendor with standing admin rights you can't see, log, or revoke on your own terms is a real
governance gap in ordinary enterprise IT too.

Here's where the regulated world demands more. In ordinary IT governance, "the vendor has
excessive access" is a security finding — serious, but a security conversation. For a validated
BECS, the same fact is also a **records-control** question with its own regulation attached, and —
this module's sharpest point — **a validation has to prove certain behaviors with an actual
test**, not just document a policy that says the system should behave that way. "We have a policy
requiring sequencing" and "we ran a test that tried to make BECS skip a step, and it refused" are
not the same evidence, and only one of them is what an inspector asks for.

## The rule in plain English

Three separate things are tangled into VAL-1203's open questions, and this module pulls them
apart.

**First: Part 11 (21 CFR Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures) only reaches records
that some other regulation already requires you to keep.** Part 11 never stands alone. It sets the
conditions under which an *electronic* version of a record is as trustworthy as paper would have
been, for a record some other regulation already made you keep. That underlying regulation —
606.160 for a blood-establishment quality-control record, 211.68 for the validation requirement
module 1 built this whole course on — is called a **predicate rule**: the rule whose records a Part
11 control exists to protect. Part 11 by itself never creates a new recordkeeping duty; it rides on
top of one that already exists. That's as far as this module takes predicate-rule doctrine. Full
treatment — how that scoping decision actually gets made and documented, and what it means for
ALCOA+ (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, plus the "+" additions) and
audit-trail review in practice — is `data-integrity-and-records`'s subject, a future course. Here,
know the term and move on.

**Second: closed and open systems are about who controls access and who's responsible for the
records — not simply about whether an outsider can reach the system at all.** A **closed system**
is one where Lakeshore's own people — the ones responsible for the content of the records on BECS
— control who gets in. An **open system** is one where that control has slipped outside the hands
of the people responsible for the records. The dividing line isn't "can anyone from outside ever
connect in." It's who's actually in charge of granting, logging, time-limiting, and revoking that
access, and whether the people responsible for the records are still the ones making that call.

Walk the vendor's remote-access request through that lens, both ways. If Lakeshore grants the
consultant's access for a defined window, logs the session, and can revoke it unilaterally — and
Lakeshore's own personnel remain accountable for what's in BECS's records — the system is still
closed, even though a vendor employee is sitting at the keyboard. If the arrangement is the one
actually proposed — standing credentials, no stated expiration, no mention of logging or
revocation — that's not an automatic "now it's open" verdict either, but it's exactly the
arrangement that drifts toward it, and toward 11.30's heavier open-system obligations. The honest
answer to "is BECS still closed" is: **it depends on exactly how this access gets built, not on
the fact that a vendor connects in at all.**

**Third: FDA doesn't enforce every word of Part 11 equally, and where its enforcement actually
lands changes what a BECS validation has to prove.** A 2003 FDA guidance (guidance tier, not
regulation) says FDA intends to exercise **enforcement discretion** on Part 11's validation
requirement and on audit trails, while naming, in the same breath, a specific list of 11.10
controls it fully intends to enforce: limiting system access, operational sequencing checks,
authority checks, device checks, training, accountability policies, systems-documentation
controls, and the open-system controls that mirror them. Those enforced controls map onto specific
11.10 paragraphs, and that mapping is this module's spine: the set of behaviors a BECS validation
actually has to *prove the system enforces*, with a test case, not a policy statement.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 11.1(a) | "Eleven point one, paragraph a" | Sets the criteria under which FDA considers electronic records and signatures trustworthy and equivalent to paper. | Why Part 11 exists at all — the baseline this whole module explains. |
| 21 CFR 11.1(b) | "Eleven point one, paragraph b" | Part 11 applies to electronic records kept under agency recordkeeping requirements, and to records submitted to FDA — not to paper records merely transmitted electronically. | Scopes Part 11 to records a predicate rule already requires, not every digital file BECS touches. |
| 21 CFR 11.3(b)(4) | "Eleven point three, paragraph b, subparagraph four" | Defines "closed system": access controlled by the people responsible for the records' content. | The exact test the vendor's remote-access proposal has to pass. |
| 21 CFR 11.3(b)(9) | "Eleven point three, paragraph b, subparagraph nine" | Defines "open system": access *not* controlled by the people responsible for the records' content. | What BECS drifts toward if the access arrangement is loose enough. |
| 21 CFR 11.30 | "Eleven point thirty" | Open systems need everything 11.10 requires, plus encryption and digital-signature measures "as necessary under the circumstances." | The heavier obligation set that follows if BECS is judged open. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(d) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph d" | Limiting system access to authorized individuals. | Base access control — for Lakeshore staff and for the vendor's remote connection alike. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(f) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph f" | Operational system checks enforcing permitted sequencing of steps and events. | The quarantine-release gate: has anyone tested that BECS actually refuses an out-of-sequence release? |
| 21 CFR 11.10(g) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph g" | Authority checks ensuring only authorized individuals can use the system, sign a record, alter a record, or perform the operation at hand. | Has anyone tested that a role without release authority actually gets refused? |
| 21 CFR 11.10(h) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph h" | Device checks on the validity of the source of data input or operational instruction. | Named here, built out in `becs-interfaces-and-data-integrity`, module 7. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(i) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph i" | Training determination for anyone who develops, maintains, or uses the system. | Ties directly to the BECS guidance's own training sentence, below. |
| 2003 guidance, enforcement list | "the 2003 Part 11 scope-and-application guidance" | Names which 11.10 controls FDA still intends to enforce despite discretion elsewhere. | The reason (d), (f), (g), (h) get a validation's real attention. |
| Guidance III.G, training sentence | "Section three, part G" | You must train personnel in system procedures (citing 211.25(a), 600.10(b), 606.20(b)). | A second, independent route to the same requirement as 11.10(i). |
| Guidance III.B, remote-access note | "Section three, part B" | Recommends logging remote access with date, time, reason, and the name of the person connecting. | The concrete answer to the vendor's remote-access request. |

## The actual text

Start with Part 11's own scope, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.1.md`:

> (a) The regulations in this part set forth the criteria under which the agency considers
> electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic
> records to be trustworthy, reliable, and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten
> signatures executed on paper.

> (b) This part applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained,
> archived, retrieved, or transmitted, under any records requirements set forth in agency
> regulations. This part also applies to electronic records submitted to the agency under
> requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act, even
> if such records are not specifically identified in agency regulations. However, this part does
> not apply to paper records that are, or have been, transmitted by electronic means.

Read (b) carefully: Part 11 attaches to records "under any records requirements set forth in
agency regulations" — that is, under a **predicate rule**. 606.160 and 211.68 (module 1's own
validation hook) are both predicate rules. Part 11 never names its own independent record; it's a
layer of trustworthiness requirements on top of a record some other regulation already made
Lakeshore keep. Full predicate-rule doctrine — how that scoping gets worked out case by case — is
`data-integrity-and-records`'s subject. Here, the term is named once, correctly, and set down.

Now the closed/open distinction, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.3.md`:

> (4) Closed system means an environment in which system access is controlled by persons who are
> responsible for the content of electronic records that are on the system.

> (9) Open system means an environment in which system access is not controlled by persons who are
> responsible for the content of electronic records that are on the system.

Neither definition says a word about where the people connecting are located, or whether they work
for Lakeshore. Both turn entirely on one question: **who controls access, and are those people the
ones responsible for the records?** A vendor employee connecting in doesn't, by itself, make the
environment "not controlled" by Lakeshore. A vendor connecting in *on terms Lakeshore can't see,
limit, or revoke* is a much closer fit for (9)'s wording.

If a system is open rather than closed, 11.30 is what follows, quoted in full from
`sources/cfr/11.30.md`:

> Persons who use open systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall
> employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, as
> appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of their creation to the
> point of their receipt. Such procedures and controls shall include those identified in § 11.10,
> as appropriate, and additional measures such as document encryption and use of appropriate
> digital signature standards to ensure, as necessary under the circumstances, record authenticity,
> integrity, and confidentiality.

Read that as 11.10's controls, plus more — encryption and digital-signature measures, scaled "as
necessary under the circumstances." It's the heavier obligation set a tightly-governed access
arrangement lets Lakeshore stay out of.

Now the 2003 guidance's enforcement posture, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/part-11-scope-and-application-2003.md`:

> we intend to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to certain part 11 requirements. That
> is, we do not intend to take enforcement action to enforce compliance with the validation, audit
> trail, record retention, and record copying requirements of part 11 as explained in this
> guidance. However, records must still be maintained or submitted in accordance with the
> underlying predicate rules, and the Agency can take regulatory action for noncompliance with such
> predicate rules.

And, in the same breath, the list of what FDA says it still fully intends to enforce:

> We intend to enforce all other provisions of part 11 including, but not limited to, certain
> controls for closed systems in § 11.10. For example, we intend to enforce provisions related to
> the following controls and requirements:
>
> • limiting system access to authorized individuals
> • use of operational system checks
> • use of authority checks
> • use of device checks
> • determination that persons who develop, maintain, or use electronic systems have the
> education, training, and experience to perform their assigned tasks
> • establishment of and adherence to written policies that hold individuals accountable for
> actions initiated under their electronic signatures
> • appropriate controls over systems documentation
> • controls for open systems corresponding to controls for closed systems bulleted above (§ 11.30)

That bulleted list maps, item for item, onto specific 11.10 paragraphs — the same ones this
module's validation lens actually sits on. Quoted in full from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`:

> (d) Limiting system access to authorized individuals.

> (f) Use of operational system checks to enforce permitted sequencing of steps and events, as
> appropriate.

> (g) Use of authority checks to ensure that only authorized individuals can use the system,
> electronically sign a record, access the operation or computer system input or output device,
> alter a record, or perform the operation at hand.

(f) is the quarantine gate in software form: can BECS actually be made to release a component
before all required results are recorded, or does it refuse? (g) is the release-authority
question: can a role without release authority actually force a release, or does BECS refuse that
too? Neither is answered by a policy document saying "only authorized staff release components."
It's answered by a test case that tries to make the system do the wrong thing and records that it
couldn't.

One more enforced control, named here because module 7 builds its real depth there, quoted
verbatim:

> (h) Use of device (e.g., terminal) checks to determine, as appropriate, the validity of the
> source of data input or operational instruction.

(h) asks whether BECS can tell where an input actually came from — is this result really arriving
from the instrument interface it claims to be from? That belongs to interface validation,
`becs-interfaces-and-data-integrity`'s subject next module. Here, know it's one of the controls
FDA's list says it enforces, and a validation eventually has to show it's proven, not just named.

11.10(e) — audit trails — is on the *enforcement-discretion* side of the same 2003 list:

> The Agency intends to exercise enforcement discretion regarding specific part 11 requirements
> related to computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails (§ 11.10 (e), (k)(2) and any
> corresponding requirement in §11.30).

This module's validation lens only needs to confirm BECS's audit trail exists and is turned on, as
a functional fact a test case can check. What it has to capture, and reviewing one in practice, is
`data-integrity-and-records`'s subject, not this module's.

11.10(i), training, is short enough to quote directly:

> (i) Determination that persons who develop, maintain, or use electronic record/electronic
> signature systems have the education, training, and experience to perform their assigned tasks.

FDA's BECS guidance reaches the same requirement from a separate direction, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/becs-validation-users-facility-2013.md`, section III.G:

> You must train personnel in the use of the system procedures (21 CFR 211.25(a), 600.10(b),
> 606.20(b)). Training should include assessing an individual's ability to understand and
> correctly use the system.

11.10(i) and this sentence are two routes converging on one requirement: personnel have to be
shown, with evidence — training records, a documented competency assessment, not a memory of
attending a session — to be competent to operate a validated system. A package that proves BECS
works but has no training evidence behind the people operating it hasn't proven the system
performs as validated in real use.

And the guidance's remote-access recommendation, quoted verbatim from section III.B, sitting
directly after its system-administrator documentation list:

> Note: Although a remote access log is not part of validation records, you may consider keeping a
> log of remote access to any part of your system, such as the BECS or laboratory instruments. We
> recommend this log include the date, time, reason for the access and the name of the person
> connecting to your system.

That's the practical answer to the vendor's remote-access request. It's guidance-tier — "you may
consider," "we recommend," not "you must" — but it's exactly the evidence that would let Lakeshore
show an inspector who controlled the vendor's access and when, which is precisely what
11.3(b)(4)'s "controlled by persons who are responsible for the content" asks someone to be able
to demonstrate.

### Reconciling this against what the curriculum already used

Two earlier lessons already cited pieces of 11.10, without this module's depth. `becs-in-the-
pipeline` named 11.10(a) — "validation... to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended
performance" — as the hook for BECS's "validated state." `directing-the-quality-analyst` used
11.10(j) (written accountability policies) as a concept. Both stay accurate exactly as written;
this module doesn't re-teach either one. What it adds is the enforcement posture layered on top:
11.10(a) is real regulatory text, but FDA's 2003 guidance exercises enforcement discretion on it
and leans on predicate rules — 211.68, 606 — to carry BECS's actual validation obligation instead,
exactly why module 1 grounded VAL-1203's validation requirement in 211.68(a), not 11.10(a). 11.10(j)
and (k)(2) sit on the guidance's discretion list alongside audit trails and stay named-only here
too. This module spends its depth on the part of 11.10 earlier lessons left alone — (d), (f), (g),
and (h) — plus naming 11.1, 11.3, and 11.30. Put together: the earlier text was always accurate;
this module says, for the first time, which pieces FDA actually enforces and which a BECS
validation has to put an actual test case against.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
reading VAL-1203's file wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has a Part 11 policy. They'd ask for three
specific things.

**A test case that actually tries to break the sequencing and authority rules, not a sentence
saying the rules exist.** For 11.10(f): did anyone attempt a release with a result still pending,
and does the record show BECS refused it? For 11.10(g): did anyone attempt a release-level action
from a role that shouldn't have that authority, and does the record show BECS refused it too? A
URS row that says "the system shall enforce proper sequencing" with no test ID behind it is a
promise, not proof — the same lesson module 1 taught about untestable requirements, applied here
to two specific regulatory behaviors.

**Evidence of who controls the vendor's remote access, and when it happened.** A standing
credential with no log is the kind of fact an inspector finds the moment they ask "show me who
connected to this server last quarter, and why." A dated access log — the guidance's III.B
recommendation, actually implemented — turns "we control the vendor's access" from a claim into
something demonstrable.

**Training records behind the people actually operating the system**, not a generic statement that
"staff are trained." 11.10(i) and the guidance's III.G sentence both ask for the same evidence:
dated, individual, tied to the procedures the person actually performs on BECS.

A bad answer to "how do you know this vendor can't do more than you've authorized" sounds like "we
trust them, they're a good partner." A good answer points to a specific access-control
configuration, a log, and a revocation mechanism Lakeshore itself controls.

## Common traps

**"11.10(a) is FDA's main enforcement hook for BECS validation."** Not quite. 11.10(a) —
validation — is real regulatory text, already named in this curriculum. But the 2003 guidance puts
11.10(a) on its enforcement-discretion list and leans on predicate rules instead. For BECS, FDA's
own guidance names 211.68 and Part 606 — not 11.10(a) — as the actual regulatory basis requiring
Lakeshore's validation. Both routes point at the same outcome, a validated system, but the
enforcement mechanism FDA actually leans on is the predicate rule, not Part 11's own clause.

**"A vendor connecting in remotely automatically makes BECS an open system."** Also not quite. Go
back to 11.3(b)(4) and (9): the test is who *controls* access and who's *responsible* for the
records, not whether an outside party can reach the system at all. A tightly governed vendor
connection — Lakeshore grants it, logs it, time-limits it, and can revoke it — can stay closed.
What's actually proposed for VAL-1203 — standing credentials, no stated logging or revocation path
— is the arrangement that drifts toward open, or at minimum leaves a control gap worth flagging
before go-live. The flip answer ("remote access means it's open") and the complacent one ("the
vendor always needs access, it's fine") are both wrong for the same reason: neither looks at who
actually controls it.

## What this means for your job

- **Before signing off on the vendor's remote-access request, ask who grants it, who logs it, and
  who can revoke it.** If the answer to any of those three is "the vendor decides," that's the
  open-system drift happening in real time, not a hypothetical.
- **Require a remote-access log for this vendor specifically, given VRA-0219's history.** The
  guidance's III.B recommendation — date, time, reason, and the name of the person connecting — is
  the record that would let Lakeshore show an inspector who controlled this access and when, if
  the question ever came up the way it did for the earlier incident.
- **Send VAL-1203's test plan back until it has an actual test case for 11.10(f) and (g), not just
  a policy statement.** A requirement that BECS "shall not permit release before all results are
  recorded" needs a test that attempts exactly that release and records the refusal. Same for a
  release attempt by an unauthorized role — flag this in the URS now, before test design locks in.
- **Keep 11.10(a) and the predicate rule straight before anyone else's confusion reaches a
  validation plan.** If a consultant cites "Part 11 compliance" as the reason BECS is validated,
  the correction is that 211.68 and Part 606 actually require it — Part 11 adds trustworthiness
  criteria on top, once a predicate rule already made the record a requirement.
- **Confirm training evidence exists for the specific people operating Release B**, not a general
  statement that staff received training. 11.10(i) and the guidance's III.G sentence both expect
  it, and it's a control area FDA's 2003 guidance says it still enforces.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Someone on the upgrade project says, "11.10(a) is FDA's main enforcement hook for BECS validation." Accurate?

Not quite. 11.10(a) is real regulatory text — "validation of systems to ensure accuracy,
reliability, consistent intended performance" — and it's the paragraph this curriculum named back
in `becs-in-the-pipeline`. But FDA's 2003 Part 11 guidance explicitly lists 11.10(a) under its
enforcement-discretion policy: FDA doesn't intend to bring an enforcement action to enforce that
specific paragraph, and relies on predicate rules instead. For BECS specifically, FDA's own BECS
guidance names 21 CFR 211.68 and Part 606 as the regulatory basis that actually requires Lakeshore's
validation. 11.10(a) and the predicate-rule-based obligation point toward the same outcome — a
validated system — but the enforcement mechanism FDA actually leans on is the predicate rule, not
Part 11's own validation clause.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The vendor's consultant wants standing, unlogged remote access to the production BECS server after go-live. Does that automatically make BECS an "open system" under 11.3(b)(9)?

Not automatically, but it's the arrangement most likely to turn into one. 11.3(b)(4) and (b)(9) turn
on who *controls* access and who's *responsible* for the records — not simply on whether an outside
party can connect at all. If Lakeshore grants the access for a defined purpose, logs it, can
time-limit it, and can revoke it, with Lakeshore's own personnel remaining accountable for what's
in BECS's records, the system can stay closed even with a vendor connecting in. What's actually
proposed here — no stated expiration, nothing said about logging or revocation — is the version of
this arrangement that drifts toward 11.30's open-system obligations, or at minimum represents a
real control gap. The fix isn't to refuse the vendor access outright; it's to require the access be
granted, logged, and revocable on Lakeshore's own terms — starting with the guidance's recommended
remote-access log.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: VAL-1203's URS still has no testable requirement for "BECS refuses an out-of-sequence release" or "BECS refuses a release by an unauthorized role." Is that a real gap, or is documenting the policy enough?

It's a real gap, and a policy statement doesn't close it. 11.10(f) (operational system checks
enforcing permitted sequencing) and 11.10(g) (authority checks restricting who can perform an
operation) are both on the 2003 guidance's list of controls FDA actually intends to enforce. That
means a BECS validation has to prove, with a test case that could actually fail, that the system
refuses an out-of-sequence release and refuses a release attempted by an unauthorized role — not
just document that Lakeshore's procedures say releases should happen in the right order by the
right people. This is exactly the kind of requirement that belongs in the URS before test design
locks in, flagged now for VAL-1203's test plan.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the map: which Part 11 controls a BECS validation actually has to prove the system
enforces, why FDA's enforcement leans on predicate rules instead of 11.10(a) itself, and how to
reason through a closed-versus-open-system question instead of answering it on reflex. Next,
`validated-state-lifecycle-and-patching` takes the upgraded, newly-live BECS through its first
periodic review and its first post-upgrade OS patch — and finally gives VIA-0842's open question,
the one this course opened with, a real answer: were those twelve targeted tests actually enough?
